name: DATEDIFF
shortDescription: Difference between dates: date1 - date2 with the dates first
description: DATEDIFF(date1, date2) is MySQL's: date1 - date2 in DAYS. With a unit, the dates first is still date1 - date2, and the unit first - the spelling of SQL Server, Snowflake, Redshift, DuckDB and Elasticsearch SQL - is date2 - date1. It counts the calendar boundaries crossed, as DATE_DIFF does.

parameters.name: date1
parameters.description: The date subtracted FROM when the dates come first; the start when the unit comes first

parameters.name: date2
parameters.description: The date subtracted when the dates come first; the end when the unit comes first

parameters.name: unit
parameters.description: Unit for result (YEAR, QUARTER, MONTH, WEEK, DAY, HOUR, MINUTE, SECOND)

examples.title: MySQL's own documented example
examples.sql: SELECT DATEDIFF('2007-12-31'::DATE, '2007-12-30'::DATE) as days FROM orders

examples.title: Days until a deadline
examples.description: Positive while the deadline is in the future
examples.sql: SELECT DATEDIFF(due_date, CURRENT_DATE) as days_left FROM tasks

examples.title: The unit first
examples.description: The month boundaries crossed from start_date to end_date, as SQL Server counts them
examples.sql: SELECT DATEDIFF(MONTH, start_date, end_date) as months FROM projects

notes: The dates first is date1 - date2, with or without a unit; the unit first is date2 - date1.

DATEDIFF counts the calendar boundaries crossed, in UTC, a WEEK starting on Monday: DATEDIFF(YEAR, '2025-12-31 23:59:59', '2026-01-01 00:00:00') is 1. For the whole units elapsed, use TIMESTAMPDIFF(unit, date1, date2).

Changed in 0.24.0: this name was an alias of DATE_DIFF; every dates-first form returned date2 - date1, and from WEEK up it counted the whole units elapsed between the two calendar dates. Swapping the dates of a statement written against the old behaviour restores its sign, not its count.
